TL;DR

The Phoenix Board approves ordinary Treasury spending, but ERIS retains the power to replace the Treasury contract’s code and owns the registry that assigns important permissions. TLA’s promised transfers of upgrade administration and configuration ownership remain incomplete. Treasury has a similar control risk, though its terms do not state the same handover deadlines.

The Board did receive upgrade control of the ampLUNA hub and bridge. Terra governance can change other administrators too; repairing internal permissions may also require cooperation or tested replacement code. The records establish retained powers and incomplete commitments, not misuse of funds.

Evidence checked 16 November 2026. This review covers 27 named Terra contracts and selected approved proposals. It does not establish a complete inventory of ERIS property or audit every transaction.

Two systems funded to manage community assets

Terra Liquidity Alliance (TLA) uses incentives and voting to support liquidity on Terra. Its development proposal describes acquired liquidity-pool positions as Community Pool assets. Phoenix Treasury receives a share of chain staking rewards through Terra’s Alliance funding mechanism and provides tools for Board-approved payments, grants and other Treasury operations. ERIS built the infrastructure for these systems.

The Board can approve payments while another authority can change the rules those payments follow. Understanding that separation is necessary to judge whether the community has received the control described in the approved terms.

Creda, Votion and Estima are application-development grants. Their funding alone does not impose TLA’s handover terms. This page focuses on the tools managing chain liquidity and Treasury funds.

Why the two proposals address contract control

The question is whether the people accountable for community assets can actually inspect, operate and recover the systems holding them.

These findings help explain the proposals’ handover and independent-review requirements. A change of director can change who votes on ordinary spending. It does not, by itself, change the Treasury’s upgrade administrator or the registry’s owner. A complete remedy needs to address both Board accountability and the separate technical powers.

Proposal 1: removal and controlled transition

Seeks 0xPhilipp’s removal and a controlled transition while preserving a minimum of three affirmative approvals. Its handover requirements matter because replacing a director alone would leave ERIS’s separate contract permissions in place.

Read Proposal 1 and its transition amendment

Proposal 2: governance and independent accountability

Can operate with the existing Board if Proposal 1 fails. Its independent financial and authority review tests grant commitments, privileged operations and milestone acceptance across all directors, with a right of response.

Read Proposal 2 and its governance amendments

How the evidence connects to the proposed safeguards

Operating roles leave other powers above them
The proposals call for records of direct and indirect privileged control, including the shared TLA registry and Foundation-used Treasury/v3 contracts. A list of Board roles alone cannot demonstrate a complete handover.
Some transfers are complete; others remain unresolved
Both preserve TLA’s original one-month administration and three-month ownership commitments. They require credit for completed transfers and a dated remedy for missing items, rather than treating the hub and bridge transfers as settlement of every control question.
A key transfer does not establish operating independence
Source, build and maintenance access, independent operating checks and a costed contingency plan are included so the Foundation can assess changes and continue operating if a maintainer becomes unavailable.

Each proposal calls for acknowledgement and named implementers within seven calendar days of passage, an implementation dossier within 21 days of passage, and weekly progress. Proposal 2’s independent review has a separate timetable: preliminary findings within 30 days and a final report within 60 days of legal adoption. A status report does not substitute for that review.

These are the 16 November discussion texts, not enacted rules. The control record supports scrutiny and a verifiable remedy; it does not itself establish misconduct, liability or the case for any particular director’s removal. Passage, legal adoption and contract execution are separate steps. Neither proposal automatically transfers keys, recovers assets, shuts down a system or transfers unrelated ERIS property.

The Board approves spending; ERIS can replace the code

A smart contract is a program on the blockchain that can hold assets and enforce rules. Phoenix Treasury is the contract at terra16st8yfprkdl06kccktshd3p2vccq93xcn9mkhjl8s4jumyjtd4kqye0me5, deployed as code 3347. It handles payments and grant milestones, scheduled or negotiated trades, and reward and delegation activity. At capture, it held 2,263,683.561738 LUNA in its bank balance, alongside other denominations. That is a gross balance: reserved grants and other claims must be reconciled before treating any amount as available to spend. It is not a total Foundation valuation.

Under the normal payment route, the Phoenix Board is the Treasury’s controller. Its four equally weighted members have a 75% approval threshold, so three YES votes are needed. Recorded veto settings also give the Think Tank and Terra governance opportunities to stop qualifying spending.

A separate permission, called upgrade administration (also called migration administration), allows a contract’s code to be replaced. The Treasury’s upgrade administrator is the address identified as ERIS in the launch terms. A compatible replacement could change who may approve spending, weaken the veto checks, or transfer spendable assets held at the Treasury address. Replacement Treasury code could stop requiring Board authorization, even while the Board’s own voting threshold stays unchanged.

That creates exposure to misuse, a compromised key or an upgrade mistake even while ordinary payments follow Board rules. It does not show that any such replacement or unauthorized transfer occurred. Control of this contract also does not give access to every Foundation wallet: staking restrictions, other contracts, liabilities and chain rules still matter.

Configuration ownership is a separate permission

The Treasury and TLA use a shared registry: a contract recording which addresses hold particular roles. Its internal owner is another address identified as ERIS. The Board holds several operating roles, but those roles do not transfer ownership of the registry. Retained transactions show the ERIS configuration address assigning the Treasury configuration role to itself and later changing the fee-collector role. The exact limits on these configuration changes in the current code still need source review.

TLA’s terms promised a time-limited ERIS role

The approved TLA launch linked terms published on 12 August 2024 that distinguished the two powers: configuration ownership would transfer to Phoenix Stewardship after three months, and contract administration after one month. Stewardship is the Phoenix body acting through the Board. The reviewed TLA contracts still name the ERIS upgrade address; the shared registry still names the ERIS configuration owner, with no pending transfer.

Those handovers remain incomplete in the 16 November records. ERIS delivered deployed infrastructure, and the Board received meaningful operating roles. Neither delivery nor those role assignments completes the promised transfers of code-upgrade and configuration authority.

Treasury made different promises

The Treasury launch promised audited open-source tooling, spending vetoes, governance control of future funding and a way for governance to reclaim unclaimed funds locked in the Treasury. Payment tooling is deployed and the veto safeguards are recorded in its configuration. A published audit covers a stated source revision; this review has not reproduced the current deployed build or exhaustively tested its safeguards.

The Treasury terms do not independently set TLA’s one-month and three-month deadlines. The concern here is whether the promised protections remain dependable while ERIS retains upgrade and registry authority, and whether the Foundation can inspect and operate the system.

For this comparison, the approved proposals, executed decisions and incorporated terms are treated as the complete agreement record. No additional agreement or amendment is assumed. Historical dollar amounts in the funding record are proposal descriptions, not current valuations or proof of payment.

Rejected TLA changes are not adopted policy

Whitelisting reform #4830 and pool relocation #4836 were rejected. Their proposed changes cannot be presented as new mandates, and rejection alone does not document repeal of the original handover commitments.

This is a control and delivery comparison, not a full grant-performance audit. Quarterly reporting, the conditional URA refund, full take-rate accounting and all later source revisions require separate reconciliation.

The hub and bridge transfers are complete at the upgrade layer

On 25 October 2026, ERIS proposal 9 transferred upgrade administration of the ampLUNA hub and CW20-ICS20 bridge to the Phoenix Board. The hub manages staked LUNA; the bridge supports token transfers between chains. The Board later used its new authority to approve and execute the hub upgrade in A292.

These transfers give the Board a powerful way to change those two contracts. Their internal permissions remained separate: the hub’s owner still points to the ERIS configuration address, and the bridge’s internal governance field still points to the ERIS upgrade address. P9 did not transfer TLA or Treasury administration.

ERIS says continued operation justified retaining control

In his 19 October response, 0xPhilipp said ERIS continued developing, maintaining and operating TLA, and considered transfer inappropriate given its concerns about the Board. He welcomed supervisor review. Keeping a system maintained is a relevant operational concern; the response does not itself document approval to extend the original handover timetable. No approved extension was identified in the reviewed records.

On 2 November, Vini supported Stewardship administration and access to source code and maintenance documentation. He expressly gave an individual view, not a collective Board decision.

Internal settings still affect users

The focused review of hub code 2726 found additional owner control over batching and unbonding timings, alongside existing fee, delegation and voting-operator settings. Poor settings could disrupt operation or delay withdrawals. The Board’s migration power provides a route to change these controls; the policy question is which settings the owner may change, under what limits and with whose approval.

P9’s execution date comes from retained primary transaction evidence; executed proposal status and current administrators were checked again. A292 is now executed, superseding older discussion-stage descriptions. The focused binary review is not a full security audit.

Open-source commitments need usable source access

A handover needs usable source code, build instructions and maintenance access. Otherwise, the Board can be accountable for community funds while depending on an outside operator to inspect a change or recover from a failure. A dispute or unavailable maintainer can then interrupt service.

The Treasury launch expressly describes an audited OSS smart contract and links its source code. OSS means open-source software. On the agreement basis used here, that is part of the promised Treasury delivery. The original Phoenix setup grant funds development and an audit; the explicit OSS wording appears in the later Treasury launch terms linked by proposal #4822.

TLA’s launch links Completed Contract Code and a completed audit. Its original development proposal funds development and auditing without an express open-source clause. The launch therefore presents public source as delivered work, but its wording is less explicit than Treasury’s about open-source status.

The reviewed texts do not specify a deadline for publishing later upgrades or an automatic penalty for withdrawing public access. The published commitments support asking for usable source; they do not provide an automatic on-chain enforcement mechanism.

The current deployments are not verified as open source

The advertised erisprotocol/contracts-ve3 public repository returned 404 again on 16 November. A follow-up check of ERIS’s public repositories and a repository-name search found no confirmed replacement source for the current Treasury/TLA deployments. That establishes an access gap at the advertised location, while leaving relocation or Foundation private access unresolved. A private copy would answer part of the operational-access question; it would still leave the public-source commitment to explain. The September 2024 Treasury audit covers a stated source revision, and this review has not reproduced a build matching the current deployment.

Governance can change control, but the remedy must reach both layers

Native Terra governance can reassign a contract’s upgrade administrator without the existing administrator’s signature. This requires an executable Terra proposal that passes and runs successfully. A Phoenix Board vote or a text-only community vote does not, by itself, make that change.

Changing the administrator alone does not require replacement contract code. It also leaves internal owners and registry roles unchanged. Those permissions need their own accepted transfer, where the existing code supports one, or a tested migration that changes the relevant state.

A migration replaces the code used at the existing contract address. A carefully designed migration can repair internal roles while retaining balances and legitimate claims. For that route, reviewed and uploaded replacement code is needed, together with a migration procedure tested against the existing storage and dependent contracts. No recovery migration has been prepared or simulated in this review.

Sudo cannot add a power the contract does not implement

A governance sudo message calls a privileged function inside a contract. It can only do what that deployed function supports. The checked Treasury code 3347 and hub code 2726 have no sudo function, so a direct sudo call cannot repair either current deployment. Other contracts need their own checks.

Alliance funding changesChange or stop the relevant reward funding through the chain’s Alliance governance mechanisms.Stopping future inflows does not transfer administrators, recover already-paid funds or settle outstanding depositor and grant claims.

A proposal must name every permission it changes

A concrete recovery proposal could first specify the intended administrators for the Treasury, the shared TLA registry and every affected dependent contract, then resolve internal owners and privileged roles through cooperative accepted transfers or reviewed migrations. Changing only the registry administrator would leave its current internal owner able to operate until that second layer is addressed. The hub and bridge already have Board migration administrators; their remaining internal permissions need separate treatment.

The downloaded Treasury and hub binaries match the chain’s recorded code hashes. Checking their available functions does not constitute a full behavioral audit.

The reviewed governance policy also permits administrator changes and migration when a contract has no administrator. Clearing an admin blocks the ordinary admin route, but does not remove this native governance recovery route.

Existing keys can act before the proposal executes

Recheck deployed code and permissions before execution, test the complete proposal on a faithful test copy of chain state, and specify post-execution checks for both administrators and internal roles. A proposal being accepted for voting does not prove its messages will execute successfully.

Governance cannot obtain missing private source or credentials merely by changing a contract field, independently certify completed work, or automatically reverse assets already transferred beyond the affected contracts. A recovery proposal must preserve legitimate user claims and be accompanied by the source, maintenance and accountability work described below.

This route was checked against the Terra v2.22.0 release reported by two public nodes and its pinned governance handlers. The supporting record contains version responses, source references and deployed binary export checks.

What these records establish about ownership

The TLA development proposal describes acquired liquidity as Community Pool assets. The reviewed funding decisions do not convey Treasury assets to ERIS. A contract field called owner records a technical permission; it does not settle legal title to the funds.

Asset ownership and technical roles

Scroll sideways to read all columns.

QuestionWhat the record establishes
Who owns the assets?The TLA development text describes acquired LP positions as Community Pool liquidity. User deposits and the tokens representing them remain subject to their protocol claims. A grant is funding for an agreed scope; balances, fees and technical permissions do not establish beneficial ownership or personal profit.
Who can replace a contract?Its migration administrator can authorize new code, subject to chain rules. This is a separate layer from ordinary spending approval.
Who can change settings?An internal owner or registry role controls the functions assigned to it by the deployed code. A field named owner is not a legal title deed.
Who can operate it?Controllers, voting operators, whitelist managers and executors have distinct permissions. Paying for development or operating a service does not by itself settle the permanent authority to govern it.

Contract register and supporting records

TLA and Treasury are the focus of this handover review. The broader 27-contract capture also retains application and ERIS-product records for context; inclusion does not establish community ownership or a duty to transfer those products.

Separate category: grants to build applications

Creda, Votion and Estima are application-development awards. The executed funding messages contain no TLA-style handover timetable. These awards are not evidence of failure to hand over TLA or Treasury.

How to verify a complete handover

Check who can approve a payment, who can alter its permissions, and who can replace the code enforcing them. A handover is complete only for the powers its executed transactions change. The proposed verification record should include:

  1. An asset and authority register: each contract, asset claim, funding source, legal owner where established, migration admin, internal owner, operator, fee recipient and downstream dependency. Confirm which settings the registry owner can change in the deployed code.
  2. An approval trail: the grant or ruling authorizing each retained power, applicable deadline, approved variation and any outstanding revenue-sharing or source-delivery obligation.
  3. Verified transfers: executed transactions and accepted ownership, followed by fresh queries of every layer. A new spending controller alone does not prove the upgrade or registry owner changed.
  4. Operational continuity: reproducible deployed builds, source/documentation access, key recovery, maintenance and tested emergency procedures.
  5. Independent limits: disclosed conflicts, independent approval of upgrades and related-party payments, appropriate delay/monitoring controls, and a published route for urgent action.

These are proposed verification requirements, not claims that governance has already enacted them. The two current discussion proposals can use this register to define what must transfer, what may remain with an operator, and which community assets need protection during transition.
